text: The otter held a dread place in the lore of Ireland. The Highland Scots held it too. It tied the creature to the realm of the dead. Folk tales named a king of the otters. They called him the Dorraghor or the Dobharch nigh. He led his colony through water. His pelt sold for a sum past any coin. A hunter learned that a white mark under the jaw was the only place a blade could bite. The rest of the hide turned every weapon. The man who killed that king paid the debt with his own life. The kin declared it so. A sliver of the pelt set near the door guarded the whole household. The same sign saved the soldiers at the rout of Culloden. Those men carried the hide as they marched. That same dread of the realm beyond runs through Welsh and Irish tale. In an old Welsh story, Arthur nearly loses his life. He tried to carry off the cauldron of plenty from the Welsh Otherworld of Annwfn. Irish legend keeps its own place for that dread. The name Dún Scáith means fort of shadow and fear. Tech Duinn serves as the house of Donn. Donn is the unnerving figure who welcomes the dead. The Welsh word Uffern now means hell. It probably grew from Christian hatred of pagan religion. Latin writers of the late twelfth century set down the word. Walter Map and Giraldus Cambrensis were those writers. The word comes from the Latin infernum. Folk tradition names several rulers of the Otherworld. They include Arawn, who contends with his rival Hafgan. Named lords include Cethem and Eochaid Iúil. In a separate district of the realm, Eógan Inbir appears with Bé Chuma at his side. The pair Labraid Luathlám with Li Ban rule another district. Mannanán mac Lir holds it together with Fand. Dáire stands with Rigru Rosclethan. Tethra rules in his own quarter. The craft-god Goibniu hosts a feast. The feast is known as Fled Goibnenn. Ale flows there without end.

okr.objective: Place the otter within Irish and Highland Scottish lore of the Otherworld and survey the rulers and places named in that dread realm.
key_results: The otter was a dread portent bound to the realm of the dead in Irish and Highland Scottish lore.
A king of the otters led his colony through water, and his pelt fetched a price past any coin.
A white mark under the jaw was the only place a blade could pierce the king otter's pelt.
A scrap of hide guarded the household and saved soldiers at the rout of Culloden.
Tech Duinn served as the house of Donn, the unnerving figure who welcomes the dead.
Arthur nearly lost his life trying to carry off the cauldron of plenty from Annwfn.
Dún Scáith marked the Irish fort of shadow and fear.
The Uffern was first written down by Walter Map and Giraldus Cambrensis in the late twelfth century, came from the Latin infernum, and is now the Welsh word for hell.

Rulers of the Otherworld include Arawn with rival Hafgan, Cethem, Eochaid Iúil, Eógan Inbir with Bé Chuma, Labraid Luathlám and Li Ban, Mannanán mac Lir and Fand, Dáire and Rigru Rosclethan, and Tethra.
The craft-god Goibniu hosts the Fled Goibnenn, an otherworldly feast flowing with endless ale.
